statement.p: To begin, we declare that \wvec_1=\vvec_1, and we call W_1 the line defined by \wvec_1.

li.p: Find the vector \vhat_2 that is the orthogonal projection of \vvec_2 onto W_1, the line defined by \wvec_1.
Form the vector \wvec_2 = \vvec_2-\vhat_2 and verify that it is orthogonal to \wvec_1.

Explain why \laspan{\wvec_1,\wvec_2} = \laspan{\vvec_1,\vvec_2} by showing that any linear combination of \vvec_1 and \vvec_2 can be written as a linear combination of \wvec_1 and \wvec_2 and vice versa.
The vectors \wvec_1 and \wvec_2 are an orthogonal basis for a two-dimensional subspace W_2 of \real^4. Find the vector \vhat_3 that is the orthogonal projection of \vvec_3 onto W_2.
Verify that \wvec_3 = \vvec_3-\vhat_3 is orthogonal to both \wvec_1 and \wvec_2.
Explain why \wvec_1, \wvec_2, and \wvec_3 form an orthogonal basis for W.
Now find an orthonormal basis for W.
We can check that \wvec_1, \wvec_2, and \wvec_3 form an orthogonal set. Since \vvec_i can be written in terms of \wvec_j and vice-versa, these new vectors form a basis for W.
We have \vvec_1 = \wvec_1 and \vvec_2 = \wvec_2 + 2\wvec_1 so a linear combination of \vvec_1 and \vvec_1 can be rewritten as a linear combination of \wvec_1 and \wvec_2.
Since \vvec_i can be written in terms of \wvec_j and vice-versa, these new vectors form a basis for W.
